sections.title: What counts as HIIT
sections.text: HIIT asks for work that is hard for your current fitness, usually followed by an easier interval that lets you put in another good effort. Heavy breathing is expected, but losing control of your technique is not. Racing through circuits does not automatically give the same training effect as structured high-intensity aerobic intervals.

sections.title: What Tabata is
sections.text: The classic Tabata format is eight rounds of 20 seconds of hard work and 10 seconds of rest, four minutes in total. The original research used very intense cycling efforts, so a casual 20/10 circuit is better called “Tabata-style” unless the effort is similar. A short protocol still needs a warm-up beforehand and recovery afterward.

sections.title: Who should start simpler
sections.text: If you are coming back after a break from activity or learning new movements, a few weeks of comfortable aerobic work first may serve you better. If you have a medical condition that could be affected, ask your doctor before starting. Burpees and jumps are not needed to make cardio intense, and a stationary bike may be safer and easier to control.

sections.title: Limit the hard work
sections.text: Start with short intervals you can complete with good form, and leave enough easy days between hard sessions. Raising frequency, intensity and rounds all at once can bring fatigue without extra benefit. HIIT is one option alongside steady activity, strength training and everyday walking, and you can get fit without it.
